Seminar Title:

Phase behavior of the P1 domain of α-Synuclein: Insights from atomistic simulations

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Physics and Astronomy

Speaker Name:

Sanchari Chakraborty ( Rollno : 520ph1001)

Speaker Type:

Student

Conference Hall (MC224) (Zoom Link: https://us06web.zoom.us/launch/jc/89963129034)

Date and Time:

05 Aug 2026 11 AM

Contact:

Mithun Biswas

Abstract:

The internal environment of a living cell is exceptionally complex and consists of an abundance of organelles. Among these are the biomolecular condensates also known as membraneless organelles (MLOs), which do not have a delimiting membrane. Formation of such phase separated compartments are regulated by interactions between the intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids, particularly RNA. Biomolecular phase separation influences multiple cellular processes, such as signaling and protein assembly, but MLOs are also implicated in numerous neurodegenerative diseases. The pathogenic aggregated states of the presynaptic IDP,&nbsp&ampalpha-Synuclein (&ampalpha-Syn) have been associated with multiple diseases such as Parkinson&amprsquos and multiple system atrophy. Several experimental and computational studies have been conducted to understand&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn structure and function. However, the sequence determinants modulating the pathogenic aggregation of&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn still remain elusive. Although the central non-amyloid&nbsp&ampbeta-component (NAC) region is known as the major driver of pathogenic assembly, recent experimental studies have identified a 7-residue segment, known as the P1 (residues 36-42) region within the N-terminal to be indispensable for&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn structure and function. The P1 region has been termed as the &amplsquomaster-controller&amprsquo of aggregation of the protein. Misfolding and subsequent self-assembly of&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn leads to the formation of liquid-like MLOs which are a precursor to fibrillation. It is likely that the P1 region modulates the phase separation of&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn as well.&nbspIn this work, we employ the crucial P1 segment as a model peptide fragment and investigate its self-assembly and thermo-responsive phase behavior. In order to obtain molecular insight into how the P1 domain phase separates, we performed all-atom molecular dynamics simulations in explicit solvent at varying temperatures. It is observed that the P1 domain can phase separate on its own above a lower critical solution temperature (LCST). Strong hydrophobic interactions steer the P1 chain assembly towards the formation of a condensed phase. Weak multi-chain interactions among the peptides reveal a dynamic inter-connected network. Tyrosine (Y39) forms the strongest contacts between pairs of residues within the dense phase. In this study, we also investigate the effect of sequence variation on the phase boundary. We particularly examine the point mutations, Y39A and S42A, since they are known to be vital for&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn oligomerization and aggregation. The results reveal that both the mutated segments can self-assemble at higher temperatures. Y39A can phase separate above an LCST and form large oligomers similar to wild-type P1. On the contrary, S42A exhibits anomalous thermo-responsive behavior and assembles&nbspinto intermediate-sized oligomers. This signifies that even though tyrosine is crucial for stabilizing the P1 chain network at lower temperatures, it is not essential for mediating condensation at elevated temperatures. The investigation of the transport properties of the systems reveals that the wild-type P1, Y39A, and S42A chain assemblies have liquid-like properties. They also show a higher mobility as the system temperature is increased. This work provides a detailed picture of how a key fragment of the&nbsp&ampalpha-Syn protein phase separates. It offers crucial insights into how certain mutations can alter the interaction network and modulate the self-assembly pathway of the disordered fragments.
